label: Invariant Geometry of Probability Distributions
notes: This chapter, printed pages fifty-one through seventy, asks which geometry on probability laws respects loss of observational detail. Coarse graining a raw outcome into a reported value is our basic stress test, and the geometry that survives it turns out to be governed by f-divergences and the Fisher information metric.

label: The Invariance Criterion
notes: Replacing an outcome x by a reported value y equals k of x pushes every law forward to the coarse alphabet. A disciplined geometry must never let this lossy report make two distributions look more distinguishable. That single demand, stated as monotonicity of divergence, organizes the entire chapter and selects its central objects.

label: Coarse Graining as a Markov Map
notes: On a finite alphabet a coarse graining is a partition: each coarse cell sums the fine probabilities inside it, giving a row-stochastic matrix with one entry equal to one per fine outcome. Monotonicity then reads as divergence of the mapped pair never exceeding divergence of the original pair.

label: f-Divergences
notes: Decomposable invariant divergences add one local contribution per outcome and take the form sum of p f of q over p, with f convex and f of one equal to zero. Adding a linear term leaves the divergence unchanged on the simplex, and the convention f double prime of one equals one fixes the scale.

label: Monotonicity is Jensen
notes: Why is every f-divergence monotone? When two fine cells merge, the new likelihood ratio is a probability-weighted average of the old ratios. Convexity of f, applied through Jensen's inequality, forces the merged contribution to fall below the weighted sum of the originals, so distinguishability can only shrink.

label: Equality and Sufficiency
notes: Equality in the monotonicity inequality is the diagnostic for sufficiency. If the within-block conditional distribution is identical for both parameter values, the coarse report discards nothing about the parameter. Our experiment confirms a vanishing residual in the sufficient case and a strictly positive gap once a hidden conditional is perturbed.

label: Standard Examples and Alpha
notes: Kullback-Leibler, its dual, Pearson chi-square, and the squared Hellinger form are all f-divergences with specific convex generators. They share an identical second-order metric but differ at higher order. Those higher-order differences are exactly what the alpha-family parameterizes, with alpha minus one, zero, and one marking familiar endpoints.

label: Fisher Metric Invariance
notes: A sufficient embedding splits coarse mass into fixed conditional weights and splits the tangent vector in the same proportions. Substituting into the Fisher quadratic form, the conditional weights sum to one and cancel, leaving the original length. This algebraic cancellation is the computational heart of Chentsov's uniqueness theorem on the finite simplex.

label: Square-Root Coordinates
notes: On the positive cone the invariant line element is sum of d m squared over m. Setting xi equal to twice the square root of m turns it into the ordinary Euclidean metric, so the probability simplex becomes a sphere of radius two. This is the Hellinger picture: the Euclidean shadow of the invariant geometry.

label: Applied Lab and Takeaways
notes: The sensor lab collapses eight fine states into four privacy bins; every f-divergence drops, the report leaking less. The chapter's lesson: coarse graining tests invariance, decomposable invariant divergences are f-divergences, equality signals sufficiency, and up to scale Fisher information is the unique invariant Riemannian metric.
